$why: Columns and tables that exist in a live store and that no committed DDL
creates. Every one was an ALTER run by hand against a database, so a store
rebuilt from source is a DIFFERENT database from the one in production --
which is how the volume ended up 14 migrations behind the laptop without
anything noticing until the census read a column that was not there.
This is a DEBT LIST, not a permission list. ETL/schema/check_store_schema.py
fails on anything not recorded here, and fails again once an entry stops
being true, so the only direction it can move is down. Clearing an entry
means writing its migration into ETL/events/load/migrations/ and lowering
'budget' by one.
'budget' is the count of entries below. It is stated separately on purpose:
deleting an entry without lowering it, or lowering it without deleting an
entry, both fail.
2026-08-08: 17 -> 3. Migrations 028, 029 and 030 create the fourteen
columns, and 008 finally has the .sql file it never had, which is why
public_equity_stakes.via_fund and public_funding_events.instrument_class
were on this list at all -- they were a migration nobody could see, not a
hand ALTER.
The list also MISSED four: scheme_code, application_url, sector_mix and
scheme_operators, which no committed statement created and which were the
only genuine hand-ALTERs among the fifteen. They are declared by 021's and
022's table rebuilds -- `CREATE TABLE funding_instruments_new (... )` --
and then SELECTed out of the table being rebuilt, so a reader of the DDL
sees them created while every store built from source dies at 021 without
them. Reading a rebuild's CREATE as a declaration is a false negative this
check still has; ETL/schema/check_schema_replay.py is what catches it, by
replaying the DDL instead of reading it.
The three that remain are tables, and they are staying. Each is created by
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS in the single script that both creates and
consumes it, so its DDL is committed and there is exactly one copy of it.
Restating a twenty-nine-column staging table in a migration would be a
second definition of the same table. If they should move, the move is to
make this check read the owning script -- not to copy the DDL.
